Construct a complete proof, not an annotation list

Construction 1. Four obligations at one checkpoint

For a loop with precondition P, guard G, body B, invariant I, and postcondition Q, first choose the checkpoint immediately before each guard evaluation. Initialisation must establish I from P. The body must re-establish I from I together with G. Exit must establish Q from I together with the negation of G. Total correctness additionally requires a well-founded decreasing measure whenever G is true, and the model must ensure that every executed expression and access is defined.

For a scan counting a key in an n-element array, use a processed half-open prefix [0,i). Define c to be the number of matches in that prefix, and keep 0≤i≤n. Initially i=c=0, and the empty prefix contains zero matches. If i<n, reading A[i] is safe. Increase c by one exactly when A[i] equals the key, then increase i by one. The newly processed prefix adds exactly that element, preserving the count and the bounds. Exit gives i=n, so c counts the whole array. The measure n−i decreases by one and remains nonnegative. The unmodified input array is part of the frame condition; without that condition, a concurrent or hidden mutation could invalidate the counted prefix.

An assertion checked only on one trace does not prove its preservation from every state admitted by I. Conversely, a true relation may be too weak to imply Q. These are different failures. Testing the scan on an empty array verifies a boundary witness; the general proof above quantifies over every nonnegative n and every possible key distribution under the stated array model. [Cornell Lecture 4; CMU Contracts; MIT state-machine invariant principle.]

Construction 2. Backward substitution includes definedness

The assignment rule for exact, defined expressions is wp(x:=E,Q)=Q[x←E]. The right-hand side refers to the pre-assignment state. For a sequence, propagate the desired condition backward through the last statement first. For a conditional, require the relevant branch precondition under each guard outcome. These rules construct admissible initial states; they do not assert that a final condition already held initially.

Suppose a program assigns y=10/x using exact real division and the desired result is y≥2. Definedness requires x≠0. If x>0, multiplying by x preserves the inequality and gives 10≥2x, hence 0<x≤5. If x<0, multiplying reverses the inequality and gives 10≤2x, which is incompatible with x<0. The weakest admissible condition is therefore 0<x≤5. Simply substituting and multiplying by x without a sign split can include invalid negative inputs or the undefined input zero.

For array writes, model the array as a map with a single updated cell. A final predicate about A[i] after writing A[j]=v must split the alias case i=j from i≠j. Valid indices do not imply distinct cells. Machine arithmetic adds further definedness or representation constraints; an abstract real or integer expression must not silently adopt finite-width behavior. [Cambridge historical assignment/array rules; CMU executable contract qualifications.]

Construction 3. A maximum needs an attaining value

To find the maximum of a nonempty ordered array, initialise best=A[0] and i=1. Use an invariant stating that best is a value in the processed prefix and is at least every value in that prefix, together with 1≤i≤n. When the next value exceeds best, replace best with that value; otherwise retain it. Either update preserves the witness and upper-bound properties. At exit i=n, best is an input value dominating the whole input, hence its maximum.

For argmin, retain an index loc in [0,i) with A[loc]≤A[t] for every processed t. Initialisation loc=0 and i=1 satisfies this on the one-element prefix. Replacing loc only on a strict improvement selects the earliest minimum when ties occur; replacing on equality too selects the latest. Both satisfy an unspecified minimum-index contract, but only one satisfies a particular tie policy.

The nonempty premise licenses A[0]. A zero initial sentinel for a general maximum changes the candidate set to the input plus zero and fails on all-negative arrays. A NaN value does not obey ordinary total-order comparisons; a floating-point application must either exclude it or define and implement a compatible order. A proof of argmin's value alone does not establish that its reported index is valid or corresponds to that value. [Cornell argmin; CMU preconditions.]

Construction 4. Logical representation controls conservation

Sorting requires order and conservation; stable sorting additionally preserves equal-key record order. During insertion, a saved key leaves a logical hole in the array. Each right shift duplicates a physical entry, so the physical array is not necessarily a permutation at an intermediate checkpoint. Exclude the hole and add the saved record to obtain the correct conserved multiset. When the saved key is placed in the hole, logical conservation becomes physical conservation again.

For [1,4,2], saving 2 and shifting 4 gives physical [1,4,4]. Excluding index 1 yields records {1,4}; adding the saved 2 restores the original multiset. The prefix-order argument must also say where larger shifted keys lie relative to the hole. Stable insertion shifts only strictly greater predecessor keys, so earlier equal records stay before the new equal record. An inclusive greater-or-equal test can keep keys sorted while reversing identities.

A merge instead has two consumed prefixes and one emitted prefix. The emitted multiset is their union, and the two unconsumed suffixes plus output preserve all input records. Sortedness of each run establishes that selecting a smaller valid head emits the smallest remaining key. When one run is exhausted, append the other safely. A proof cannot compare an exhausted head or assume an undefined sentinel value. The particular program determines its intermediate representation; a generic “the array stays sorted and unchanged” annotation is insufficient. [Stanford insertion/merge; Cornell interval representations.]

Construction 5. Well-founded progress is more than numerical decrease

A natural-valued measure V that is nonnegative at the loop checkpoints and strictly decreases on every guarded transition cannot support an infinite execution: each descent consumes at least one natural step. For a two-boundary partition, V=gt−i is ideal because every branch reduces it exactly once. A body may revisit the same physical index after a swap while still making one unit of logical progress.

A positive real measure can decrease forever. Starting at x=1 and repeatedly dividing by two gives xk=2−k>0 for every finite k. The guard x>0 never becomes false under exact real semantics, even though x decreases and approaches zero. Finite floating-point underflow changes the program model and cannot be imported into that exact proof.

A lexicographic pair of naturals can prove termination when a lower-priority coordinate resets. For example, from (1,0) choose any finite B and move to (0,B), then repeatedly decrement the second coordinate until (0,0). The first coordinate decreases at the reset, making the lexicographic pair smaller regardless of B; afterward the second decreases. Every chosen execution is finite, but there is no uniform bound independent of the unrestricted B. Termination, a per-input runtime bound, and a bound uniform over all nondeterministic choices are distinct claims. [MIT well-founded state-machine progress; Cambridge historical variants.]

Construction 6. Certificates meet a bound with an actual witness

For minimisation, a feasible witness of cost U gives OPT≤U. A verified lower bound L applicable to every feasible solution gives L≤OPT. If L=U, the candidate is optimal. Neither direction establishes uniqueness. The witness and bound must refer to the same instance and objective.

For source distances, require d(s)=0, edge inequalities d(v)≤d(u)+w(u,v), and an s-to-v path attaining d(v) for each claimed finite distance. Summing inequalities along any path telescopes to d(v)≤that path's cost, providing the universal lower bound. The attaining path supplies the opposite bound, proving equality. Parent equalities alone are not paths: a parent cycle can satisfy every local equation while failing to reach the source. A decreasing rooted-depth certificate or an independently checked root-reaching walk repairs that missing condition.

Negative edges do not invalidate telescoping. A negative-total cycle does: summing its inequalities would imply zero is at most a negative number. Reachability and the definition of allowed walks determine which source-distance claims are affected. The certificate framework is independently derived from the reviewed invariant and contract methods; it is not attributed to a graph course that was only listed rather than read. Question 43 proves the bound/witness argument numerically, and Questions 44–47 test all three graph obligations with concrete counterexamples.

Contracts, states and the meaning of correctness

A state gives values to variables and identifies the current control location. For arrays, it also gives each indexed value; for mutable objects, it records shared references. A program command maps an initial state to an execution that may terminate normally, fail, or continue indefinitely. A mathematical pseudocode model uses exact integers unless a finite arithmetic model is explicitly declared.

A precondition P describes the admitted initial states. A postcondition Q describes the required final state. The notation {P}C{Q} here means partial correctness: every normally terminating execution from a state satisfying P ends in a state satisfying Q. It says nothing about a nonterminating execution. We establish safety separately, so the absence of normal termination through an error cannot count as a useful correctness certificate. Total correctness means partial correctness together with termination for every admitted input; our complete algorithm claims also require safe evaluation of every expression and array access.

For a sorting routine, “the result is sorted” is an incomplete contract. A routine returning an empty array satisfies that sentence for every input. Let A0 be an immutable snapshot of the initial array, and let bag(A) denote its multiset of values, including multiplicities. A complete value-level contract is:

bag(A)=bag(A0)

For every valid adjacent index, meaning 0≤i<n-1, require:

A[i]≤A[i+1].

The quantified set is empty when the array has fewer than two elements. Stability is an additional contract: equal-key records retain their original relative order. If the procedure sorts in place, its frame condition must also specify which memory it may modify. Correctness of a sorted list of keys does not establish correctness of record identities, payloads or external aliases.

Specifications can be inconsistent or too weak. An impossible precondition makes a partial-correctness triple vacuously valid. A postcondition that merely says “the output is an integer” does not specify exponentiation. Before proving anything, identify the input domain, mathematical function, permitted mutation, empty-input convention and tie rule.

Example: two meanings of exponentiation. Over exact integers, the result of input (3,6) is 729. Under arithmetic modulo 256, the corresponding residue is 217. A proof of one result does not prove the other. Unsigned finite-width arithmetic, signed arithmetic and arbitrary-precision arithmetic must not be interchanged silently. In C, unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo its range; signed overflow is not defined as ordinary modular wrapping.

Backward reasoning and verification conditions

Suppose a pure assignment is x = E, and the expression is defined in every admitted state. To establish a desired postcondition Q, substitute the old expression E for every free occurrence of the assigned variable in Q. This is substitution in the logical formula, not substitution of a newly computed value into the old expression. Bound variables must be renamed if necessary to avoid capture.

wp(x:=E,Q)=Q[E/x].

For example, after x = x + 3, the requirement x2=25 becomes (x+3)2=25, hence old x=-8 or old x=2. A forward guess such as x=5 refers to the final state and is not the required initial condition. Over fixed-width arithmetic, this algebra must be repeated in the specified arithmetic model and include any safety obligation.

For a sequence, reason backward from the final command first:

wp(C1;C2,Q)=wp(C1,wp(C2,Q)).

For x = x + 1; y = 2*x, and final requirement y=10, the second assignment requires 2x=10, so the first requires 2(x+1)=10, giving initial x=4. Initial y is irrelevant because it is overwritten. Reversing the substitution order gives the wrong state relationship.

For a total, pure Boolean guard B:

Write the two guarded requirements separately:

F1=(B⇒wp(C1,Q)),
F2=(¬B⇒wp(C2,Q)).

The conditional's weakest precondition is their conjunction F1∧F2.

The guard is evaluated in the initial state of the conditional. For if x < 0: x = -x, the omitted else branch is skip. Thus x≥0 afterward follows both when initial x<0 and when initial x≥0. In machine signed integers, negating the minimum representable value requires separate analysis; the exact-integer proof alone does not justify the implementation.

The consequence rule permits a stronger precondition and a weaker postcondition. If P'⇒P, the known triple {P}C{Q} applies to P'; if Q⇒Q', its result implies Q'. The directions matter. Proving correctness for positive inputs does not prove it for all integers. Proving the exact result does imply a looser result bound, but a loose bound does not identify the exact result.

An array update must account for aliasing of indices. For A[i] = v, model the new array as a functional update: its value at j is v when j=i, and old A[j] otherwise. In A[i]=1; A[j]=2, the desired postcondition A[i]=1∧A[j]=2 requires i≠j, assuming both indices are valid. Treating the two indexed cells as automatically distinct is an invalid proof.

A verification condition is a mathematical implication whose validity establishes one proof obligation. For a loop with guard B and invariant I, the partial-correctness conditions are:

P⇒I,
{I∧B}C{I},
I∧¬B⇒Q.

Add obligations for a defined guard, safe body operations, termination of the body and a well-founded decrease. A failed verification condition may mean the program is wrong, but it may instead mean the annotation is too weak or unsuitable. For example, annotating while False with an invariant False fails initialization even though the command immediately terminates and leaves the state unchanged.

How to read the revised diagrams

A proof or arithmetic derivation advances through justified dependencies; formulas are native MathML. Bar height is value magnitude; stable labels identify records during moves and swaps. Place-value bits, quotient groups and arithmetic certificates expose the numeric representation. An indexed sorted strip exposes both half-open boundaries and their shrinking distance. Explicit subproblem/dependency edges expose splitting, evaluation and aggregation. Vertices, arrows and relation edges show actual membership, dependence or reachability.

Use the next-step control to inspect a completed transition. The caption states the assumptions and the exact state; a finite trace illustrates, but does not replace, the general proof. Record indices, logical boundaries, time coordinates and electrical polarity have distinct meanings.

Invariant discovery and termination

An invariant belongs to a specified checkpoint, normally just before the guard. Statements about the state halfway through the body may differ. To discover an invariant, rewrite the final goal as a relationship between processed data, unprocessed data and immutable inputs. Then add bounds sufficient to establish safety and an exit implication. Useful components include conservation laws, prefix properties, interval exclusion and snapshots of overwritten values.

Inductiveness is stronger than truth on reachable states. A predicate may hold at every reachable checkpoint but fail to be preserved at an unreachable state satisfying that predicate. Verification conditions quantify over all states allowed by the invariant; strengthening it can exclude those spurious states. Conversely, a transition-preserved predicate that is false initially tells us nothing about reachable states. The negation of an invariant is not automatically an invariant.

For total correctness, choose a variant in a well-founded set. A nonnegative integer V that strictly decreases on each executed body permits at most initial V iterations. The variant need not reach zero: the guard may become false sooner. A nonnegative real that decreases strictly can have an infinite sequence, such as 1,1/2,1/4,…. A nonnegative integer that merely never increases can also remain constant forever.

For nested progress, lexicographic pairs of nonnegative integers are useful. The pair (a,b) decreases if the first coordinate decreases, or if it stays equal and the second decreases. A decrease of a may reset b to any finite nonnegative value. Such a measure proves termination, but initial a+b need not bound the number of steps. If a program can nondeterministically reset b to arbitrarily large finite values, there may be no uniform step bound determined by the initial pair alone.

Counterexample discipline. To disprove a universal claim, give one admitted input, trace the relevant states, identify the failed obligation and state which hypothesis would repair it. Testing many inputs is evidence about those inputs. A proof establishes a quantified claim under its assumptions. Neither should be presented as the other.

Binary search with empty arrays and duplicate keys

The lower bound of a target t in a sorted array is the first index whose value is at least t, or n if no such value exists. This differs from finding an arbitrary equal element. Duplicates therefore belong to the contract, not to an optional afterthought.

def lower_bound(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if a[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

At the checkpoint, use these three clauses:

0≤lo≤hi≤n,
∀i<lo:A[i]<t,
∀i≥hi:A[i]≥t,

where the quantified indices are valid array indices. The unclassified interval is [lo,hi). Initialization holds because both classified ranges are empty. If lo<hi, floor midpoint selection gives lo≤mid<hi, so the access is safe.

If A[mid]<t, sortedness implies that every earlier array value is also less than t. Moving lo to mid+1 therefore classifies the entire discarded left region correctly. The old right classification remains unchanged. Otherwise A[mid]≥t, and sortedness makes every later value at least t; assigning hi=mid establishes the right classification.

Let L=hi-lo. The first branch produces L'=hi-mid-1; the second produces L'=mid-lo. Both lie between zero and ⌊L/2⌋. Hence L is a nonnegative integer variant and the loop terminates. At exit lo=hi, so the two classified regions exhaust the array. This proves the first eligible index, including the all-small case lo=n and the empty-array case lo=0.

For nonempty intervals the maximum number of body executions is ⌊log2n⌋+1, equivalently ⌈log2(n+1)⌉; an empty array requires zero. This counts body executions in this exact implementation, not arbitrary binary-search implementations. Depending on the target, some branches end sooner.

The tempting update lo = mid is wrong here. With A=[2] and t=3, it preserves the classification invariant but leaves the interval unchanged. Partial correctness cannot supply the missing termination argument. The midpoint expression also illustrates model dependence: lo + (hi-lo)//2 avoids adding the two endpoints, but the implementation still needs a type capable of representing the endpoints, their difference and all assigned values.

Sorting proofs that preserve records

Insertion sort: the saved-key hole

def insertion_sort(a):
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key = a[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] > key:
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
        a[j + 1] = key

At the outer checkpoint, the prefix A[0:i] is sorted and contains exactly the records initially in that prefix; the unprocessed suffix has not changed. The inner loop cannot use the assertion that the physical array remains a permutation after every assignment. A shift duplicates a value while the saved key temporarily lives outside the array. Instead regard position j+1 as a logical hole. The other prefix positions plus the saved key contain the original prefix multiset.

The portion left of the hole remains sorted. Every record shifted right has key strictly greater than the saved key, and its relative order with other shifted records is preserved. When the guard becomes false, either j=-1, or A[j]≤key. Filling the hole yields a sorted prefix of length i+1 and restores physical multiset equality. The inner variant is j+1 at a true guard; every shift decreases it by one. The outer loop has finitely many positions.

With tagged records (2,a),(1,b),(2,c), processing the last record with a strict greater-than comparison leaves (2,a) before (2,c). Replacing > by >= can move the newer equal-key record ahead of an older one. Sortedness and multiplicity survive, but stability does not. Comparison equality must be evaluated on keys, while assignments carry the full record.

Merge sort: two distinct inductions

To prove merge sort, first prove a merge lemma: given two sorted input sequences, merging them returns a sorted multiset union. At a merge checkpoint, the emitted prefix is sorted, every emitted value is no greater than each next available head, and the emitted prefix plus both unconsumed suffixes preserves the total input multiset. Consume the smaller head; consume the left head on equality when stable sorting is required. When one side is exhausted, append the remaining sorted suffix.

The merge variant is the number of unconsumed records across both inputs. Appending a tail can be viewed as repeated safe emissions. Array access requires testing exhaustion before comparing heads. A proof that assumes both heads exist cannot justify the final phase of the algorithm.

Now use strong induction on input length. Length zero or one is already sorted. For larger lengths, split into children of lengths ⌊n/2⌋ and ⌈n/2⌉, both strictly smaller than n. The induction hypothesis proves both child contracts. The merge lemma proves the parent contract. The length measure proves recursive termination. The runtime recurrence is a separate analysis; solving a recurrence does not establish that the returned sequence has the right order.

Partitioning without skipping unclassified elements

For three-way partitioning around a pivot p, maintain four regions:

A[0:lt]<p,A[lt:i]=p,A[i:gt] unknown,A[gt:n]>p.

Here a relation on a slice means it holds for every value in that slice. The bounds are 0≤lt≤i≤gt≤n. Start with lt=i=0, gt=n, and repeat while i<gt.

def partition3(a, pivot):
    lt, i, gt = 0, 0, len(a)
    while i < gt:
        if a[i] < pivot:
            a[lt], a[i] = a[i], a[lt]
            lt += 1
            i += 1
        elif a[i] > pivot:
            gt -= 1
            a[i], a[gt] = a[gt], a[i]
        else:
            i += 1
    return lt, gt

In the less-than branch, when lt<i, the old element at lt belongs to the equal region, so moving it to the old scan position preserves the enlarged equal region. When lt=i, the swap is a self-swap and both boundaries advance together. In the greater-than branch, the incoming value from the old end of the unknown region remains unclassified. Advancing the scan index would skip it; keep i unchanged. The variant gt-i decreases by exactly one in all branches. Swaps preserve the multiset, and at termination no unknown element remains.

This procedure partitions; it does not sort either outer region. It is not stable in general. For arrays containing unordered values such as floating-point NaN, the three comparison cases may not have the assumed trichotomy. The exact ordered-key model must be stated.

Arithmetic algorithms and their domains

Division by repeated subtraction

For nonnegative integer X and positive integer Y, initialize q=0,r=X and repeatedly execute r = r - Y; q = q + 1 while r≥Y. The invariant is:

X=qY+r,q≥0,r≥0.

The body preserves conservation because (q+1)Y+(r-Y)=qY+r. The guard ensures the new remainder remains nonnegative. Since Y≥1, the variant r strictly decreases. At exit 0≤r<Y, which uniquely characterizes quotient and remainder. The number of body executions is ⌊X/Y⌋.

If Y=0, the conservation equality alone remains true and the guard stays true, but the remainder never decreases. If Y<0, the remainder grows under subtraction. Thus the positive-divisor assumption is a termination requirement and part of the mathematical division convention. Cambridge's worked partial-correctness derivation deliberately separates these obligations; it must not be read as a total-correctness proof for every divisor.

Euclid's algorithm

For integers a≥0,b≥0, use while b != 0: a,b = b,a % b, with simultaneous assignment. At each checkpoint,

gcd(a,b)=gcd(a0,b0)

and both variables remain nonnegative. Every common divisor of a,b divides a-qb, and every common divisor of b,a-qb divides a, so the gcd is preserved. Euclidean remainder gives 0≤amodb<b for a positive divisor. The old b is therefore a decreasing variant. At exit b=0, the gcd equals final a. Adopt the explicit convention gcd(0,0)=0 if that input is admitted.

Sequentially writing a=b; b=a%b destroys the old dividend: the second assignment now computes bmodb=0. A temporary variable or simultaneous assignment is essential. Bounds on division cost and exact bit complexity belong to runtime analysis, not to this gcd correctness proof.

Exponentiation by squaring

def power(x, y):
    assert y >= 0
    r, b, e = 1, x, y
    while e > 0:
        if e % 2 == 1:
            r *= b
        b *= b
        e //= 2
    return r

For exact integers and nonnegative exponent, use rbe=xy and e≥0, with immutable original x,y. In this algorithm the exponent-zero value is defined as one, including x=0. If old e=2k, the new product is r(b2)k=rb2k. If old e=2k+1, it is (rb)(b2)k=rb2k+1. The update of the accumulator must use the old base. At exit e=0, the invariant gives r=xy.

For positive e, floor halving strictly decreases it. For y>0, the number of loop iterations is ⌊log2y⌋+1; the number of accumulator multiplications is the population count of y in binary. This displayed implementation squares the base once per iteration, including the final iteration. An optimized implementation may avoid that last square without changing the result.

The unnecessary final square also matters to machine safety. With a signed 32-bit type, base 50,000 and exponent one, the mathematical result 50,000 is representable, but squaring the base creates 2,500,000,000, beyond the signed positive range. Thus representability of the final answer alone does not prove safety of every intermediate operation.

For modulus M≥1, reduce the initial base and each product modulo M, initialize r=1modM, and replace equality by congruence. The same even/odd proof establishes the residue. When M=1, the result is zero even for exponent zero. In a narrow machine type, multiplying two residues may overflow before reduction; modular algebra does not justify an unsafe intermediate product. Exact arithmetic, a sufficiently wide intermediate, or a proved overflow-safe modular multiplication routine is required.

Certificates and choosing a proof method

A certificate is additional information that lets a verifier check a claimed result. It need not reveal how the result was found. For sorting, check nondecreasing order and multiset preservation; checking only order accepts a constant array. A permutation of original record indices provides a direct witness that every input record appears exactly once. Its indices must be distinct, in range and consistent with the claimed output values.

For a finite weighted directed graph, a shortest-path certificate illustrates the difference between feasibility and optimality. Suppose all vertices under discussion are reachable from root s. Supply distances d, a parent chain ending at s for every other vertex, and d(s)=0. Each parent edge must exist and satisfy

d(v)=d(parent(v))+w(parent(v),v)

. Every graph edge must satisfy:

d(v)≤d(u)+w(u,v).

Summing these inequalities along any root-to-vertex path gives d(v) no greater than that path's weight. Summing the parent equalities gives an actual path of weight d(v). Together, they establish optimality. The parent relation must be acyclic and reach the root; a zero-weight cycle of parents supplies equalities but no root path. Negative edge weights do not invalidate this certificate argument, but a reachable negative cycle prevents a finite certificate satisfying all edge inequalities. Unreachable vertices require separate reachability and infinity conventions and are outside this finite-distance presentation.

For a rooted tree, structural induction is often simpler than a mutable-state invariant. For a recursive function, prove each child is smaller in a well-founded measure and use its complete contract, including preservation. For a greedy optimization algorithm, a local invariant can establish feasibility while optimality still requires an exchange or dominance argument. For dynamic programming, correctness requires an induction over the dependency order and proof that the recurrence covers every admissible decision. These are proof-method boundaries; the full greedy and dynamic-programming methods receive their own later chapters.

Claim Appropriate evidence Frequent invalid replacement
Exact output of an iterative procedure State invariant, exit implication and termination A runtime recurrence
Recursive correctness Base cases, smaller children and composition lemma A trace of one recursion tree
Optimality Feasibility plus an upper/lower bound meeting a witness Feasibility alone

Mathematical and conceptual problem bank

The bank contains four authentic examination translations and 50 original or independently worded course-derived problems. Questions require exact calculations, formulas, boundary analysis and proof obligations. Full solutions are expandable for reading convenience and open automatically for printing. Original difficulty labels are qualitative medium/hard judgments; they are not measured student-performance statistics. Cross-topic authentic items are used to develop output, index and structural certificates, not relabeled as questions explicitly asking for Hoare logic.

Authentic examination questions

Question 1. A recursive algorithm with reversed concatenation

Authentic examination · English translation

Phd CE 1405 · Q9 · PDF page 3. Independently derived solution; not an official key.

For an array of distinct values, SplitSort chooses its median m, recursively processes R={x:x>m} and L={x:x<m}, and returns concatenate(SplitSort(R), [m], SplitSort(L)); arrays of length at most one are returned unchanged. What is the output order?

1.

Descending up to the median, then ascending.

2.

Approximately random.

3.

Ascending.

4.

Descending.

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 4. Prove the recursive contract and the joining order. Assume distinct input values in a total order. The base inputs of size at most one are already descending. For a larger input, the pivot m separates a greater-value block R and a smaller-value block L. Strong induction gives descending outputs from both smaller recursive calls. Every value returned from R exceeds m, and every value returned from L is below m. Consequently, joining R's output, then m, then L's output establishes descending order both inside the blocks and across their boundaries.

With values {1,2,3,4,5} and pivot 3, the greater block returns [5,4] and the smaller block returns [2,1]. The joining operation produces [5,4,3,2,1]. The alternative claiming an ascending suffix changes one recursive contract without any corresponding change in the code. The random-order alternative ignores both comparisons. An ascending output would require joining the smaller block before the pivot before the greater block.

For the stronger claim that the output is a permutation, use a median that is an actual input order statistic, choosing an input middle value for even lengths. Strict partitioning then retains every nonpivot value exactly once and the singleton pivot retains the remaining value. An arithmetic-average median for an even input can insert a new value and violate conservation, even though joining order remains descending. Equal input keys would likewise require an explicit equality block to retain all copies. The source asks about distinct-key order; state extra premises when proving a stronger contract. Input sizes strictly decrease above the base region, proving recursive termination.

Question 2. Recursive reverse-stride copying

Authentic examination · English translation

MS CS 1393 · Q167 · PDF page 34. Independently derived solution; not an official key.

Copy every other element of an N -element array a, starting at its last element, into array b from index zero upward. Call store(N-1,0). Which pseudocode is correct? Syntax below treats parameters as integers and arrays as available in the procedure.

1.

if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1);

2.

if(n<0)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1);

3.

if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+2);

4.

if(n<0)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+2);

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 1. Relate each recursive call to a copied prefix. At the kth active call, let k start at zero. The intended parameter relation is n=N−1−2k and i=k. The previously copied output prefix then satisfies b[t]=a[N−1−2t] for 0≤t<k. If n≥0, writing b[i]=a[n] adds exactly the next required source entry at the next contiguous destination position. Calling store(n−2,i+1) restores the same relation with k increased by one.

For N=6, the write pairs are (source,destination)=(5,0),(3,1),(1,2). The next call has n=−1 and returns before reading. This constructs [a[5],a[3],a[1]], exactly every other element from the end in reverse stride. For N=5, the sources are 4,2,0; for N=0, the initial n=−1 immediately returns. The destination must have room for ⌈N/2⌉ elements, and the arrays' intended separation must avoid overwriting unread source data.

Option 2 writes to b[i+1], leaving index zero unwritten and shifting the compact result. Option 3 advances i by two, leaving gaps. Option 4 combines both defects. The negative source guard must precede the read because −1 or −2 can occur in the base call, depending on parity. A natural measure counting remaining stride positions decreases at each active call, so exactly ceiling(N/2) writes occur and one additional base call terminates the recursion. A proof of output order must track both source and destination; decreasing only the source index does not establish compact storage.

Question 3. Leaf weights in a binary tree

Authentic examination · English translation

Phd CE 1405 · Q3 · PDF page 2. Independently derived solution; not an official key.

For each leaf x at depth d of a binary tree T, put w(x)=2−d. If L is the set of all leaves and α=∑x∈Lw(x), which is always correct?

1.

α=1.

2.

α≤1.

3.

α>1.

4.

α<1.

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 2. Distribute a unit of mass and allow missing children. Give the root mass 1. At each possible child edge, transfer half the parent's mass. A leaf at depth d then receives exactly 2−d. When both children exist, their two budgets sum to the parent's budget. When only one exists, half the budget is left unused. Leaves terminate their own budget without duplication. Therefore the total leaf mass cannot exceed the root's mass 1.

A structural induction makes the inequality precise for finite trees. A root leaf has mass 1. With two subtrees, each subtree's relative leaf mass is at most 1 by induction; scaling each by 1/2 gives a total at most 1. With one subtree, scaling its mass by 1/2 gives at most 1/2. This proves the bound, including all finite shapes, and does not assume that the tree is balanced or complete by levels.

Equality holds in a finite full binary tree, where every internal node has two children, including the single root leaf. A root with one leaf child has total mass 1/2. These witnesses refute both the always-equal and always-strict alternatives. A total greater than 1 contradicts the proved allocation bound. In a finite tree, a missing child at any internal node produces a positive deficit, so equality characterizes fullness. The simple conservation proof supplies a useful upper bound even when the actual leaf depths and tree balance are unknown; extra structural claims must follow from the equality premises rather than from intuition about tree size.

Question 4. Exact count of ordered triples

Authentic examination · English translation

Phd CS 1405 · Q20 · PDF page 8. Independently derived solution; not an official key.

Assume the variables have types large enough for the following code. What is the final value of Cod?

Cod = 10;
for (i = 1; i <= 15; i++)
  for (j = i; j <= 15; j++)
    for (k = j; k <= 15; k++)
      Cod++;
1.
610
2.
690
3.
630
4.
710
Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 2. Count dependent iterations and then add initialization. One increment occurs for each weakly ordered triple 1≤i≤j≤k≤15. The map (i,j,k)↦(i,j+1,k+2) is a bijection to strictly increasing triples chosen from {1,…,17}. Its inverse subtracts one from the second coordinate and two from the third. Thus the number of increments is (173)=17·16·15/6=680. Cod starts at 10, so it ends at 690.

An independent count fixes j. There are j choices for i and 16−j choices for k. Summing gives ∑j=115j(16−j)=16∑j=115j−∑j=115j2=16·120−1240=680. Both derivations preserve the equality cases in the loop bounds. The triple (1,1,1), for example, is a genuine execution and would be lost by counting only strictly increasing original indices.

The other numerical alternatives disagree with both exact counts. Counting 15³ ignores the dependent bounds; choosing three distinct numbers from 15 omits repetitions; returning only 680 omits initialization. An accumulator invariant can say that Cod equals 10 plus the number of completed innermost visits at the current checkpoint, making conservation of the count explicit. The granted wide-type premise must cover loop-index increments as well as Cod. A narrow implementation can overflow on a terminating update after the last useful body visit even when all useful indices were representable; the mathematical loop count does not by itself certify its machine translation.

Question 5. Backward substitution through a quadratic

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

Over exact integers, execute x = x + 3. What is the weakest precondition for final x2=25?

1.

x=5 or x=−5

2.

x=2 or x=−8

3.

x=8 or x=−2

4.
x=2
Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 2. Derive the set of all admitted initial states. Let u denote the initial x-value and v the final one. The assignment establishes v=u+3. The requested postcondition is v2=25, so the exact precondition is (u+3)2=25. Factoring gives (u−2)(u+8)=0, and over the integers this is equivalent to u=2 or u=−8. The forward checks are 2↦5↦25 after squaring and −8↦−5↦25.

Weakest means that every admitted initial state which achieves the postcondition is included, and no failing state is included. Option 4, initial x=2 alone, is sufficient but stronger: it excludes the valid state −8. Option 1 lists final x-values rather than their preimages. Initial 5 produces final 8, whose square is 64; initial −5 produces final −2, whose square is 4. Option 3 reverses the shift: initial 8 produces 11, and initial −2 produces 1, so neither achieves square 25.

The assignment rule substitutes the old expression into the desired final predicate. It does not assert that the final value was already true before execution. This derivation assumes exact integer addition and squaring; a machine-overflow model would require separately defined expression semantics and safety. Here the necessary-and-sufficient initial-state set is established algebraically, while the two forward traces verify its particular witnesses.

Question 6. Sequence order changes the precondition

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

Execute x=x+1; y=2*x; x=y-3 over integers. Which initial condition is weakest for final x=7?

1.
x=4
2.
x=5
3.
y=10
4.
x=10
Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 1. Reverse the statements' order when propagating requirements. Label initial values x0,y0. The first command produces x1=x0+1. The second overwrites y with y1=2x1. The last overwrites x with x2=y1−3. Therefore the entire sequence satisfies x2=2(x0+1)−3=2x0−1. Final x=7 requires 2x0−1=7, giving x0=4. The initial y-value is unconstrained because it is overwritten before any use relevant to the result.

Backward substitution obtains the same result in three proof steps. The last statement requires y−3=7, hence y=10 immediately before it. The middle statement requires 2x=10 immediately before that statement. The first then requires 2(x+1)=10 in the original state. Substituting in forward order would mix these different checkpoints rather than implement the sequencing rule.

For initial x=4, the state trace is x=5, then y=10, then x=7. Option 2's x=5 produces final x=9, so it is false. Option 3 constrains initial y=10 but permits, for instance, initial x=0, which yields final −1; the overwritten initial y cannot ensure the target. Option 4 confuses the intermediate y=10 with initial x: initial x=10 returns 19. Since the equation has one integer solution and initial y is irrelevant, x=4 is the weakest condition, not merely a sufficient example. Expression evaluation and arithmetic are exact under the question's model.

Question 7. Simultaneous versus sequential assignment

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

Initially (x,y)=(5,8). Compare simultaneous (x,y)=(y,x+y) with sequential x=y; y=x+y. What are their respective results?

1.

(8,13) and (8,13)

2.

(8,16) and (8,13)

3.

(8,13) and (8,16)

4.

(5,13) and (8,16)

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 3. Keep an explicit old-state snapshot. Simultaneous assignment evaluates both right-hand expressions before changing either coordinate. With old (x0,y0)=(5,8), it computes x1=y0=8 and y1=x0+y0=13, so the result is (8,13).

Sequential execution instead completes the first assignment before evaluating the second expression. After x=y, the state is (8,8). The next command y=x+y now uses x=8 and y=8, giving (8,16). Both programs terminate safely in this exact integer example; their disagreement is a functional-semantic difference, not a termination failure.

Option 1 treats the second sequential right-hand side as if it could still read the overwritten 5. Option 2 swaps the two assignment semantics. Option 4 leaves the first simultaneous coordinate at 5 even though its right-hand expression is old y=8. The needed repair for sequential code is a saved old x-value: store old_x=x, execute x=y, then y=old_x+y. That realizes the same state transformer as simultaneous assignment, provided old y has not also been overwritten prematurely.

In a general state, the two transformers are (x,y)↦(y,x+y) and (x,y)↦(y,2y). They agree exactly when old x equals old y, so agreement on such a test input would conceal the semantic difference. The concrete unequal input makes the lost dependence visible. A proof should name which expressions use old values and which use the updated state; unindexed variable names alone can hide an incorrect substitution.

Question 8. Conditional weakest precondition

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Course-derived analogue: Cambridge conditional verification, PDF pages 52–53

For integer x, execute if x<0: x=-x; else: x=x+2. Which condition is weakest for final x≥3?

1.
x≠0
2.
x≥1
3.
x≤−3
4.

x≤−3 or x≥1

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 4. Combine the guarded preimages of the postcondition. In the true branch, old x<0 and the new value is −x. To obtain new x at least 3 requires −x≥3, equivalent to x≤−3. This already implies the true-branch guard. In the false branch, old x is nonnegative and the new value is x+2. Its requirement x+2≥3 reduces to x≥1, which already implies the false-branch guard.

The complete weakest condition is the union of these admitted branch-specific regions: x≤−3 or x≥1. Equivalently, the conditional rule requires both implications, from x<0 to −x≥3 and from x≥0 to x+2≥3. Every integer satisfying the union follows its appropriate branch and achieves the target. The excluded integers −2, −1 and 0 produce final values 2, 1 and 2, respectively, so no excluded state can be added while preserving correctness.

Option 1, x nonzero, admits −1 and −2 and is therefore insufficient. Option 2 includes only the nonnegative successful branch and unnecessarily excludes −3. Option 3 includes only the negative successful branch and unnecessarily excludes 1. These last two are individually sufficient but not weakest. Values −3 and 1 both produce final 3 and confirm that the boundary inequalities are inclusive. This is exact integer reasoning. In a finite signed type, negating the minimum value would additionally require a safety premise, even though it satisfies the abstract negative-branch inequality.

Question 9. Which consequence direction is sound?

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

A known triple has precondition x≥0 and postcondition r=x2. Which replacement is always justified by consequence alone?

1.

Precondition true; postcondition r=x2

2.

Precondition x≥2; postcondition r≥0

3.

Precondition x≥0; postcondition r>x

4.

Precondition x<0; postcondition r≥0

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 2. Restrict assumptions and relax conclusions in the sound directions. The consequence rule takes a known triple {P}C{Q} and justifies {P'}C{Q'} when P'⇒P and Q⇒Q'. Here initial x≥2 implies initial x≥0. The established postcondition r=x² implies r≥0 over exact integers regardless of the final x-value. Therefore the option's stronger precondition and weaker postcondition are both justified.

Option 1 expands the admitted initial domain to include negative x-values. The old contract makes no guarantee there. A program returning a correct square on nonnegative inputs and an arbitrary value on negative ones would satisfy the known triple while violating the proposed stronger claim. Option 4 similarly replaces the admitted domain by x<0, which does not imply the known precondition.

Option 3 demands r>x, which does not follow from r=x² in general: final x=0 gives r=0 and final x=1 gives r=1, so strict inequality fails. Even if some particular implementation avoids those final states, consequence alone cannot infer that additional fact from the stated postcondition. No runtime or termination assertion is added by this logical rule; it transforms the functional triple under its original interpretation.

The word always is decisive. One is not allowed to inspect an unspecified implementation and invent stronger guarantees. The two implication obligations are sufficient for every command satisfying the original triple. A changed domain or a stronger result may be true for a special command, but it needs another proof rather than this consequence application.

Question 10. Array aliasing is a logical condition

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Course-derived analogue: Cambridge array updates, PDF pages 19–22

Both indices are valid. Execute A[i]=1; A[j]=2. Which is the weakest condition on indices for final A[i]=1 and A[j]=2?

1.
i<j
2.
i>j
3.
i≠j
4.

No condition

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 3. Treat array writes as updates to one shared map. The first write establishes A[i]=1. The second writes 2 at index j. If i and j differ, the second update leaves A[i] unchanged and establishes A[j]=2, satisfying both final equalities. If i=j, the second write overwrites the very cell just set to 1, leaving its final value 2. The simultaneous final requirements A[i]=1 and A[j]=2 then demand one integer cell equal two distinct constants, which is impossible.

Thus inequality of the indices is both necessary and sufficient under the already stated valid-index premise. Option 1, i<j, is sufficient but excludes valid states with i>j. Option 2 is similarly sufficient but excludes valid states with i<j. Option 4 admits i=j and fails. This explains why the weakest condition is inequality rather than an ordering of positions.

Formally, the final array A2 is the update of A1 at j, and A2[i] equals 2 if i=j and equals A1[i]=1 otherwise. This piecewise evaluation is the array-assignment analogue of backward substitution. Initial array values are irrelevant because the two required cells are overwritten, but the shared identity of a cell remains relevant. Validity only ensures the accesses are defined; it does not establish that they refer to different locations. For object references or memory pointers, the corresponding proof obligation is nonaliasing of the modified locations, which must be justified separately from address validity.

Question 11. An inductive invariant can be too weak

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original state-machine analogue informed by MIT §5.4

Start at (x,y)=(0,0) and repeatedly assign both coordinates simultaneously to (x+1,y+1). Is I:x≥0 by itself inductive under the transition, and is it sufficient to prove final x=y?

1.

Inductive and sufficient

2.

Inductive but insufficient

3.

Not inductive but sufficient

4.

Neither

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 2. Separate inductiveness from sufficient strength. At the initial state (0,0), x≥0 holds. In any state satisfying x≥0, the simultaneous transition produces x'=x+1≥1, so it preserves the predicate. This preservation reasoning quantifies over every state allowed by the predicate, regardless of y. Consequently x≥0 is inductive for the specified transition.

However, x≥0 alone does not imply x=y. The state (1,0) satisfies it and violates equality. Even if that state is unreachable from the specific initial pair, it is admitted by the chosen annotation, so the annotation cannot establish the desired postcondition by a simple exit implication. The actual reachable states are (k,k) for nonnegative integer k. Their equality needs the additional invariant x=y, which holds initially and is preserved because both coordinates increase by the same amount.

The conjunction x=y∧x≥0 therefore describes the required relation and the useful bound. Options 1 and 3 incorrectly assert that the weak predicate suffices. Options 3 and 4 incorrectly deny preservation, since adding one cannot make a nonnegative integer negative. A failure of postcondition implication must not be reported as a failure of invariant preservation.

No loop guard or stopping condition is specified in the state-machine question. Equality is established at every reachable checkpoint, but the invariant alone cannot prove that a final checkpoint is eventually reached. Correctness of a relation, sufficiency for a postcondition and termination are distinct obligations.

Question 12. Reachable truth need not be inductive

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard

Original state-machine analogue informed by MIT §5.4

Start at x=0. The transition maps zero to zero and maps every positive x to −1. Which describes I:x≥0?

1.

False on a reachable state

2.

True on every reachable state but not inductive

3.

Inductive but false initially

4.

A proof that every state is reachable

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 2. Reachable-state truth is weaker than inductiveness. Starting from zero, the transition returns zero. Every subsequent reachable state is therefore zero, so x≥0 is true at every reachable checkpoint. This conclusion follows by induction on the number of transitions: the base is zero and the only reachable successor is again zero.

To test whether the predicate is inductive, however, consider all states satisfying it, not only reachable ones. The positive state x=1 satisfies x≥0 and is mapped to −1, which violates it. Hence the predicate is not preserved on its full annotated domain. The transition on negative inputs is irrelevant to this counterexample because both the initial counterexample state and the reachable states lie in the explicitly defined nonnegative part of the transition system.

Option 1 is false because no negative state is reachable from zero. Option 3 is false twice: initialization is true and preservation is false. Option 4 confuses an invariant assertion with a reachability characterization; this machine actually reaches only zero, not every integer. A stronger invariant x=0 excludes the positive spurious states, is true initially and is preserved by the transition. It therefore supplies an inductive proof of the reachable-state property.

The example shows why a verification-condition failure does not always exhibit a bad actual execution. Its x=1 counterexample refutes the proposed preservation condition but is not reachable from the stipulated initial state. Strengthening the annotation can eliminate that proof failure without changing the command. In contrast, a reachable counterexample would refute the claimed execution property itself.

Question 13. A defective annotation does not condemn a program

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Course-derived analogue: Cambridge Exercise 45, PDF page 58

Annotate while False: x=0 with invariant False, initial assertion True, and final assertion True. Which claim is correct?

1.

The program diverges

2.

The final assertion is false

3.

Initialization of the chosen invariant fails, although the program is correct

4.

Every chosen invariant proves every loop

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 3. Identify the failed proof obligation before judging the code. The loop guard is the Boolean constant False, so the body never executes. The program behaves as skip: it terminates immediately and leaves the state unchanged. Under initial assertion True and final assertion True, the actual command is correct for every state.

The chosen invariant False nevertheless fails initialization. That verification condition is True⇒False, which is invalid in every state. Preservation is vacuously valid because its premise contains the conjunction of invariant False and guard False. The exit implication is also vacuous because its premise contains invariant False. Two vacuous obligations cannot compensate for the failed initialization condition.

Choose invariant True instead. Initialization becomes True⇒True. Preservation still has an impossible true-guard premise, and exit reduces to True⇒True. There is no body transition needing a decreasing variant; the fixed false guard directly proves termination. This repaired annotation proves the same unchanged program.

Option 1 incorrectly predicts divergence despite the never-entered guard. Option 2 contradicts the stipulated tautological final assertion. Option 4 treats an annotation as an arbitrary magic proof rather than a predicate that must satisfy concrete obligations. The correct diagnosis is a failed annotation, not a counterexample execution. This distinction matters in larger proofs: a noninductive or initially false predicate can cause verification to fail even when a different, more suitable predicate would establish the command's real contract. One must inspect initialization, preservation and exit separately before concluding that the implementation is wrong.

Question 14. A loop with exact iteration count

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

For positive integer n, initialize x=n and execute while x>0: x=max(0,x-3). How many body executions occur?

1.
⌊n/3⌋
2.
⌈n/3⌉
3.
n
4.
⌈(n−1)/3⌉
Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 2. Derive the complete state formula. After k executed bodies, the value is xk=max(0,n−3k). The base k=0 gives the initialized n. If the current positive value is n−3k, the next body subtracts three and clamps at zero, giving precisely max(0,n−3(k+1)). Once zero is reached the guard is false, so no further body occurs.

The stopping index is the least integer k with n−3k≤0, namely ⌈n/3⌉. Write n=3q+r with r in {0,1,2}. If r=0, q bodies reach zero exactly. If r=1 or 2, q bodies leave that positive remainder and one additional body clamps it to zero. Thus the exact count is q for r=0 and q+1 otherwise.

Option 1 omits that final partial subtraction when n is not divisible by three. Option 3 counts one decrement per body instead of up to three and fails at n=3, where there is one body. Option 4 fails at n=1, predicting zero even though the initial guard is true and one body is required. The question counts body executions; the final false guard adds one more guard evaluation in a straightforward while implementation. The positive-n premise excludes zero, though extending the same code to n=0 would correctly yield zero bodies. The state formula explains exact work, while nonnegative integer descent independently certifies termination.

Question 15. Strict decrease over reals is insufficient

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original termination analogue informed by MIT §5.4

Start x=1 and repeat while x>0: x=x/2 in exact real arithmetic. Which is correct?

1.

The loop terminates after one step

2.

It terminates after finitely many steps because x decreases

3.

It does not terminate; nonnegative real strict descent is not well-founded

4.

It violates x≥0

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 3. The arithmetic domain changes the termination argument. In exact real arithmetic, after k bodies the value is xk=2−k. This is strictly positive for every finite integer k. The guard x>0 therefore remains true after every finite number of bodies, and the loop never terminates.

At the same time the sequence is strictly decreasing and nonnegative. The problem is not failure of those properties; it is failure of well-foundedness of the proposed order on nonnegative reals. Infinite strictly descending real chains exist. Convergence to zero as k tends to infinity is a limiting statement, not attainment of zero at a finite program step.

Option 1 predicts a zero after one body, but the first result is one-half. Option 2 applies a rule valid for a nonnegative integer measure decreasing by at least one to a real measure with ever smaller drops. Option 4 denies the genuine nonnegativity property; every finite state is positive. The correct answer identifies precisely which termination hypothesis is missing.

A finite floating-point implementation can eventually underflow or round to zero under some formats and modes. Integer division would also behave differently, giving zero from integer one divided by two. Neither observation answers the exact-real question. A valid general repair is to use a guard x>epsilon for a fixed positive threshold, or to specify a well-founded discrete progress measure tied to an appropriate finite stopping condition. Merely relabeling the unchanged real x-value as a variant does not establish the missing finite descent property.

Question 16. Lexicographic descent and step bounds

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard

Original termination analogue informed by MIT §5.4

A pair of nonnegative integers starts at (1,0). One reset chooses any finite nonnegative integer B and changes it to (0,B). Thereafter, while its second coordinate is positive, each step decrements that coordinate by exactly one. Execution stops at (0,0). Which is true?

1.

Every execution terminates, but there is no uniform step bound from the initial pair alone

2.

Some execution has infinitely many decrements after the reset

3.

Every execution has at most one step

4.

The pair does not decrease lexicographically

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 1. Quantifier order distinguishes two different bounds. The first step lowers the first coordinate from one to zero and may raise the second from zero to any chosen finite B. This is a strict lexicographic decrease because the first coordinate decreased. With first coordinate now fixed at zero, subsequent decrements strictly lower the nonnegative integer second coordinate until it reaches zero. Each execution therefore has one reset step followed by finitely many decrements.

If decrementing means subtracting one each time, its exact length is B+1 transitions, including the reset. For every proposed finite uniform bound K depending only on the initial pair (1,0), choose finite B>K. The resulting admitted execution exceeds K. Thus every execution has a finite length, but no single finite K bounds all executions from that initial state. Formally, for every chosen finite B there exists a finite run length; one cannot interchange that with existence of a uniform bound for all B.

Option 2 incorrectly turns an arbitrarily large finite B into an infinite integer value. No permitted reset chooses infinity. Option 3 ignores the subsequent B decrements and fails already at B=1. Option 4 denies lexicographic decrease because it inspects only the increasing second component; lexicographic order first compares the first component.

A potential x+y is not monotonically decreasing at the reset and cannot supply the asserted initial-sum bound. A uniform bound could be restored by a specified upper bound on allowed B, which would yield that bound plus one transitions. The stated well-founded lexicographic proof establishes termination without inventing such an additional restriction.

2.
c0+n3
3.
c0+(n+23)
4.
(n+23)
Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 3. Count the weakly ordered triples and retain the offset. Each increment corresponds to one triple 1≤i≤j≤k≤n. Map it to the strictly increasing triple (i,j+1,k+2) in {1,…,n+2}. Conversely, a strict triple (u,v,w) maps to (u,v−1,w−2), satisfying the original weak inequalities. The map is a bijection, so the increment count is (n+23) and the final accumulator is c0+(n+23).

For n=2, the four triples are (1,1,1), (1,1,2), (1,2,2), and (2,2,2), matching (43)=4. This small case exposes why repeated indices must count. Selecting three distinct original indices would instead count (n3), which is wrong. Multiplying n³ ignores the order constraints and includes many forbidden triples. Omitting c₀ counts work but does not give the requested final value.

An independent sum groups by j: there are j possible i-values and n−j+1 possible k-values, giving ∑j=1nj(n−j+1)=n(n+1)(n+2)/6. At n=0, no body executes and the accumulator remains c₀; the polynomial also gives zero increments. The exact arithmetic model must support every loop-index update as well as the accumulator. The bijection proves a formula for dependent loops without assuming their bounds are independent.

Question 51. Recursion depth as an index invariant

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

Copy indices N−1,N−3,… from an input into consecutive output cells starting at zero. For N=10, what final copied source index and output length occur?

1.

Source zero; length five

2.

Source one; length five

3.

Source one; length six

4.

Source zero; length ten

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 2. Derive the indices from the recursive parameters. With N=10 and initial call store(9,0), the source–destination pairs are (9,0), (7,1), (5,2), (3,3), and (1,4). The next call has source index −1 and returns before accessing either array. There are five copied elements, and the last copied source index is 1.

At the kth active call, starting with k=0, the parameters satisfy n=N−1−2k and i=k. An access occurs precisely while n≥0. For N=10, that allows k=0,…,4. The caller must allocate at least ⌈N/2⌉=5 destination positions. The source indices lie in [0,N), and the negative termination call has no read because the guard is checked first.

An option ending at source index zero uses the even-index sequence rather than every other index starting at the odd last index 9. Counting six includes the base call as if it wrote an element. A destination increment of two leaves gaps and does not implement compact copying. For an odd N, the last copied source index is zero; for an even positive N, it is one. For N=0, the initial source index is already −1 and no element is copied. Safety and the index relation explain all these cases together.

Question 52. An exact invariant determines a nonlinear sum

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Course-derived summation analogue: Cambridge for-loop verification, PDF pages 57–58

Initialize s=0, k=1. While k<=n, execute s += 2*k-1; k += 1, with exact integers and n≥0. Which invariant at the checkpoint just before the guard is correct?

1.
s=k2
2.
s=(k−1)2
3.
s=2k−1
4.
s=n2
Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 2. Match the sum to the next unprocessed index. With s=0 and k=1, the invariant is s=(k−1)2. It holds initially because both sides are zero. One body adds 2k−1 and then increments k. The new sum is (k−1)2+(2k−1)=k2, which equals (k'−1)2 because k'=k+1. Thus the equality is preserved.

To derive the final result, also keep the bounds 1≤k≤n+1 for an integer n≥0. The guard k≤n implies that advancing k preserves the upper bound. On exit k>n, the integer bounds force k=n+1, and the equality gives s=n². The variant n−k+1 is nonnegative at every guard checkpoint and decreases by one in each body. At n=0, initialization gives k=1, the guard is false, and s=0=n².

An invariant s=k² fails at initialization. An expression involving (k+1)² is offset in the wrong direction. A claim about the target n² alone is not the useful intermediate relation because it normally holds only at completion. The equality without bounds is insufficient to infer the exit value of k, and it says nothing by itself about termination. This example shows how a functional relation, range information, guard, and progress measure cooperate in a complete proof.

Question 53. An induction hypothesis must include preservation

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard

Original strengthening of Stanford recursive proof

For a recursive sorting proof, the induction hypothesis says only that each child output is sorted. Which additional assertion is essential to establish the complete parent sorting contract?

1.

The child runtime is linear

2.

Each child output preserves its input multiset

3.

The recursion tree is balanced

4.

Every input key is positive

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 2. Strengthen the recursive contract before composing it. A child routine that merely returns sorted data could replace every input value with zero and satisfy that weak condition. A parent that merges those sorted results would then return a sorted array containing the wrong values. Therefore sortedness of each child result is insufficient to prove that the whole recursion sorts the original input.

The required child contract includes preservation of the child's complete input multiset. For a split into left and right parts, their original multisets combine to the parent's multiset. By strong induction, both child outputs are sorted and preserve their own inputs. A correct merge then returns a sorted output whose multiset is the union of those child outputs, hence exactly the original parent's multiset. If stability is promised, the split order and merge's tie policy require additional proof.

Termination needs strictly smaller recursive inputs above a complete base region; none of these content properties alone proves it. An alternative adding only a runtime bound does not recover lost values. An alternative requiring both children to return identical arrays would be unjustified for different inputs. An alternative claiming sortedness alone is enough is refuted by the all-zero implementation. Strengthening an induction hypothesis is legitimate when one also proves that strengthened statement at the base and induction steps; it cannot simply be assumed because the parent needs it.

Question 54. A smallest counterexample to a weakened contract

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

A claimed maximum routine initializes best=0 and scans a nonempty integer array using best=max(best,a[i]). Which input refutes its contract, and what invariant does the code actually maintain?

1.

[−2]; best is the maximum of zero and the processed values

2.

[2]; best is the minimum of processed values

3.

[0]; best is undefined

4.

[]; the input satisfies the nonempty precondition

Read the full derivation, boundary cases and option diagnoses

Correct option: 1. The initialization introduces an extra candidate. A maximum routine initialized with best=0 and updated only by larger encountered values returns zero on the nonempty input [−2]. The true maximum is −2, which is the only input element. The routine's actual invariant is that best equals the maximum of zero and the processed values, not necessarily the maximum of the processed values alone.

The faulty method works for inputs containing a nonnegative maximum, which can conceal the defect in ordinary positive examples. Its failure on one admitted all-negative input refutes universal correctness. Returning zero also fails the witness property that a maximum of a nonempty finite input must be one of that input's values.

For a contract admitting arbitrary nonempty numeric arrays, initialize best to A[0] and begin scanning at index 1. Then the processed prefix is nonempty, best is one of its values, and no processed value exceeds best. Each comparison preserves those properties, and at the final index the prefix is the whole input. An alternative repair using a negative-infinity sentinel requires a type and comparator that support that sentinel, plus appropriate handling of NaN or other non-total values. An empty-input contract needs a separately defined result; neither A[0] initialization nor an unexplained zero return defines a maximum of an empty set.
